newsitem.title: PERU: IRON -- Peru's only producer sees turn in fortunes.
newsitem.headline: IRON -- Peru's only producer sees turn in fortunes.

text.p: Peru's only iron producer, Shougang Hierro Peru, has overcome nagging problems with both its workers and the government this year to emerge as a company improving output and attracting such prominent business partners as South Korea's Hyundai Corp..

A recent series of good news for Shougang signals a turnaround in fortunes for the company, which earlier in the year became the scapegoat of the country's anti-privatization lobby, according to analysts and government officials.
Jorge Kawamura, who led a government team negotiating a new investment program for the Chinese firm, said the troubled past was behind Shougang and the future looked bright.
"The company is now on the right track," Kawamura said. "Shougang has all the right intentions and it seems the company can now only go forward."
Shougang Corp, China's state iron company, bought Peru's state-run Hierro Peru S.A. and its facilities at Marcona, 250 miles south (400 km) of Lima, in November 1992 for $120 million.

However, under the terms of the sale, the accompanying $150 million investment commitment - to be carried out within three years - was not legally binding and the company had only injected $35 million by mid-1996, Kawamura said.
A media diatribe against Shougang for its low investment saw the company launch a counter-offensive publicity campaign and swiftly move to negotiate a new deal with the government.
After the bad publicity, the first good news for Shougang came earlier this month when the company announced it had agrred an investment program with the government to spend $137 million up to 2000.
This was quickly followed by further positive news that Shougang had signed a letter of intent with Hyundai to build a 300 megawatt (MW) electricity plant costing $300 million.
Local analysts acknowleged the confidence shown by the mighty Hyundai corporation was a sign Shougang had turned the corner.
The company's upturn has been registered most notably in an improvement in monthly year-on-year production, which has increased for the first time in over a year.
Shougang's July output was up nine percent to 233,854 tonnes, compared to the same month last year, according to latest Energy and Mines figures.
This reversed a trend that had seen production fall 20 percent to 1.932 million tonnes in Jan-July of this year.
And "the investment plans should mean production goes up and up," Kawamura added.
Analysts also noted the recent news for Shougang was encouraging but were cautious about a new dawn just yet.

"There has been a string of positive news for the company in the last few weeks," said Miguel Palomino, local analyst at Merril Lynch. "But a few swallows do not make a summer. We have to watch to see if things continue going forward."
It remains to be seen if the company's labor problems, which are less intense at the moment than they had been earlier in the year, have been resolved for the medium- and long-term, Palomino added.

A thorn in the company's side, which has not completely disappeared, is Shougang's perennial problem with a headline- grabbing labor union. Albeit with little grass-root support, the union is used to demanding better pay by calling for work stoppages and hunger strikes.
However, now that the anti-privatization lobby has quieted, the company's unions have lost the platform to launch their complaints from.
If Shougang can avoid further problems with unions, the company's investment plans could result in a "substantial increase" in production, the Merrill Lynch analyst said.

The company's investment commmitment is principally directed at the construction of a new pellet production line but will also increase the amount of copper extracted as a sub- product, Kawamura said.
The new pellet line expected to start up in 1999 should double output of pellets to six million tonnes per year, according to Shougang's general manager Raul Vera La Torre.

The company has excused its history of lower year-on-year production due to the modifications neeeded to produce more pellets. The reduced overall iron output has been the result of a deliberate policy to take advantage of the pellets' greater profitability.
-- Lima newsroom, 511 221-2134
